expected_answer: Use the defineModel() macro in the child (Vue 3.4+); the compiler expands it to a modelValue prop and an update:modelValue event that is emitted when the local ref is mutated.
No: computed getters must be free of side effects such as async requests; use a watcher (watch), which runs a callback with side effects when reactive state changes.
Use the v-html directive, since mustaches render plain text; rendering untrusted HTML enables XSS, so only use v-html on content known to be safe.
Yes: export a reactive() object from a module and import it in each component; with SSR this singleton store is shared across requests, which causes cross-request state pollution.

defineAsyncComponent accepts a loadingComponent option, but async components are suspensible: inside <Suspense> their own loading, error, delay and timeout options are ignored and the Suspense #fallback slot is shown, unless suspensible: false is set.
Reactive props destructure is supported from Vue 3.5 on.
Name composables in camelCase starting with "use", e.g. useMouse.
Use defineEmits with a runtime declaration or a type declaration, e.g. defineEmits<{ (e: 'change', id: number): void }>() or the named tuple syntax.
Pass flush: 'post' to watch or watchEffect (or use watchPostEffect) so the callback runs after Vue has updated the DOM; alternatively await nextTick() inside the callback.
Add the .lazy modifier: v-model.lazy syncs on the change event instead of input.
Give inject() a default value as its second argument, so the injection works without a provider.
By default v-for patches elements in place and keeps DOM/child state per position; give each item a unique key so Vue can track and reorder the elements.
Use the v-once directive; the whole sub-tree is skipped on all future updates.
Register an onMounted() hook in setup; it runs after the initial render once the DOM nodes are created.

Destructuring a primitive property from a reactive() object (or assigning it to a local variable) disconnects it from reactivity tracking, which works over property access; keep the object or use refs.
